newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa exporters seek increase in payments.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa exporters seek increase in payments.

text.p: Ivory Coast exporters will meet government officials next week to push for increases of up to 25 percent in the bareme payment structure for the 1996/97 cocoa season, bank and trade sources said on Thursday.
But little more than five percent was likely to be granted, international bankers added.

"Their overall demand will be more like 10 to 15 percent," one banker told Reuters. "Inflation is running at three percent, and that is a guideline, but there will be some new elements in the bareme, such as extra insurance costs."

Exporters said their industry forum GPEX would meet Caistab marketing board and government officials when new Caistab president Yves-Marie Koissy, appointed last month from the International Monetary Fund, arrived from Washington around 10-11 October.
"Three percent is all well and good but employee, truck and other general cost rises in the past two years have not been reflected in the bareme," said a major exporter.
Bankers said internal transport costs had probably risen more than other costs. Petrol went up by about five percent late last month and prices for imported spare parts remained high.
The bareme is a system of guidelines for producer price and remuneration for each step in the cocoa and coffee marketing chains from farmer to transporter, buyer and exporter.

The 1996/97 bareme was also likely to reflect an allowance for 25 CFA per tonne guarantees now arranged by exporters, said one international banker. The Caistab stopped giving export guaranteees as part of current donor-sponsored market liberalisation.
"It is a demand of the GPEX," said an exporter.

Bankers also foresee an adjustment for exporters' losses since the introduction of the Caistab's automated auction market in May. "They will debit for that, otherwise losses will be passed down to farmers," one said.
Exporters have complained that two European-backed firms had been bidding unrealistically high prices to secure export contracts and other firms had been unable to compete.

The auction system allocates contracts in two daily sessions to the highest bidder for the full amount on offer. It is now being reviewed by Ivory Coast and donor World Bank and European Union agencies.

Shipping sources say freight rates are unlikely to be changed. Cocoa shipments were frozen between October and mid-November 1995 when shipping lines refused to cut some rates by 25 percent as proposed by the Caistab.

The 1995/96 official list of cocoa marketing costs from farm to port included a farmgate price of 315 CFA francs, up-country buyer commission of 348 CFA, cocoa transported, bagged and ready for export at 401 CFA, exporter commission and store-to-ship charges of 415 CFA, with an extra 160 CFA per kg export tax giving a fob price of 575 CFA.
